source.subject: Biology
source.unit: Unit 1 — Diversity in the Living World
source.source_scope: Only the content printed on PDF page 1 (printed page 10): Chapter 2 opening passage on early attempts at classification, Aristotle, the Two Kingdom system, and the chapter section list.

questions.question: Who was the earliest to attempt a more scientific basis for classification of living organisms?
questions.explanation: The chapter opening states that Aristotle was the earliest to attempt a more scientific basis for classification.
questions.source_text: Aristotle was the earliest to attempt a more scientific basis for classification.

questions.question: Aristotle used simple morphological characters to classify plants into:
questions.explanation: Aristotle's plant groups were trees, shrubs and herbs, based on simple morphological characters.
questions.source_text: He used simple morphological characters to classify plants into trees, shrubs and herbs.

questions.question: Aristotle divided animals into two groups on the basis of:
options: Presence or absence of a cell wall
Presence or absence of a backbone
Presence or absence of red blood
questions.explanation: He divided animals into those which had red blood and those that did not.
questions.source_text: He also divided animals into two groups, those which had red blood and those that did not.

questions.question: Early attempts to classify organisms were instinctive and mainly arose from the need to:
options: Compare cell structure under a microscope
Use organisms for food, shelter and clothing
questions.explanation: The passage says early classification did not use scientific criteria but came from a need to use organisms for food, shelter and clothing.
questions.source_text: borne out of a need to use organisms for our own use – for food, shelter and clothing.

questions.question: In Linnaeus' time, the Two Kingdom system of classification recognised which kingdoms?
questions.explanation: The Two Kingdom system included all plants and animals under Plantae and Animalia respectively.
questions.source_text: a Two Kingdom system of classification with Plantae and Animalia kingdoms was developed

questions.question: The Two Kingdom classification did not distinguish between which of the following pairs?
questions.explanation: The page lists these three pairs as distinctions the system failed to make. Plants and animals were the two kingdoms it did recognise.
questions.source_text: This system did not distinguish between the eukaryotes and prokaryotes, unicellular and multicellular organisms

questions.question: Why was the two kingdom classification found inadequate?
options: It had too many kingdoms to remember
A large number of organisms did not fall into either the plant or the animal category
It was based only on molecular data
questions.explanation: The passage says many organisms fitted neither category, so the system was found inadequate.
questions.source_text: a large number of organisms did not fall into either category.

questions.question: Besides gross morphology, which characteristics were felt necessary for classifying organisms?
questions.explanation: The passage lists cell structure, nature of wall, mode of nutrition, habitat, methods of reproduction and evolutionary relationships. Local names are not mentioned.
questions.source_text: a need was also felt for including other characteristics like cell structure, nature of wall, mode of nutrition

questions.question: Which kingdoms have remained a constant under all the different classification systems?
questions.explanation: The page says the plant and animal kingdoms have been a constant, though the groups included under them have changed.
questions.source_text: Though plant and animal kingdoms have been a constant under all different systems

questions.question: Which statement about classification systems is supported by the passage?
options: Classification has never needed to change
The number and nature of kingdoms have been understood differently by different scientists over time
All systems have recognised exactly two kingdoms
The plant and animal kingdoms were replaced entirely in later systems
questions.explanation: The passage says classification systems have undergone several changes and views on the number and nature of other kingdoms have differed.
questions.source_text: the number and nature of other kingdoms have also been understood differently by different scientists over the time.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The Two Kingdom classification was found inadequate.
Reason (R): A large number of organisms did not fall into either the plant or the animal category.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.explanation: Both statements are given on the page, and the second is the reason the first was concluded.
questions.source_text: a large number of organisms did not fall into either category.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
1. Aristotle used simple morphological characters to classify plants.
2. Aristotle divided animals into those with red blood and those without.
3. Linnaeus' Two Kingdom system clearly distinguished prokaryotes from eukaryotes.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 match the passage. Statement 3 is false because the Two Kingdom system did not distinguish eukaryotes from prokaryotes.
questions.source_text: He used simple morphological characters to classify plants ... those which had red blood and those that did not. ... This system did not distinguish between the eukaryotes and prokaryotes

questions.question: According to the section list on the chapter opening page, section 2.4 is:
questions.explanation: The opening list runs from 2.1 Kingdom Monera to 2.6 Viruses, Viroids and Lichens, with 2.4 being Kingdom Plantae.
